hints: Focus on the difference between the two ends of a phospholipid: the phosphate head loves water while the fatty acid tails avoid it, so ask what makes the head so attracted to water.
Remember what creates polarity in biology: separation of charge, so think about what happens to an acidic phosphate group when it is surrounded by water.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two parts of a phospholipid**

Think of a phospholipid like a tadpole. It has a phosphate head and two fatty acid tails.

The tails are non-polar and hydrophobic. The head is polar and hydrophilic. We need the cause of that polarity.

**Link charge to polarity**

Polar means uneven charge distribution. A molecule becomes strongly polar when it carries full charges.

In biology, the best way to get full charges is ionisation, when a group loses or gains $H^+$ ions.

**Apply this to phosphate in water**

The phosphate group is acidic. In water it releases $H^+$ and becomes ionised with a negative charge.

That charge makes the head polar, so it is attracted to polar water molecules. That is why C is the cause, not the result.

options.A: Hydrogen bonds do form between the head and water, but that is the result of polarity, not the cause of it.
options.B: This is the opposite of the truth. The phosphate heads are soluble in water, which is why they are called hydrophilic.
options.C: Correct. The phosphate group becomes ionised in water, gaining a negative charge, and this charge separation makes it polar and hydrophilic.
options.D: No covalent bonds form between phosphate heads and water. The attraction is through hydrogen bonds and charge interactions.
